architectural_implications.after: Architecture inside commodity domains is a baseline to be adopted, not designed; differentiation budget is redirected to novel mechanisms, data, and delivery.
architectural_implications.before: Architecture and implementation detail are treated as evidence of team capability and as a source of advantage.
architectural_implications.consequence: Design reviews should ask 'is this domain commodity, and if so why are we authoring it?' rather than evaluating the quality of an authoring effort that any agent reproduces.
architectural_implications.observation: Agent harnesses standardize how a problem is decomposed and implemented, compressing inter-team variance in the resulting architecture.

architectural_implications.after: The pipeline needs an explicit reuse-discovery and differential-advantage gate ahead of the generation step.
architectural_implications.before: Search/selection was relatively costly, so building a tailored implementation was often the rational local default.
architectural_implications.consequence: Engineering process gains a mandatory pre-generation stage (search existing implementations, state what you uniquely have, name the deployment surface), enforced by tooling rather than good intentions.
architectural_implications.observation: Generation is cheap and evaluation/search is comparatively expensive, inverting the historical build-vs-find order.

architectural_implications.after: The first design is effectively free, so review/critique/redesign of agent output becomes the load-bearing human stage.
architectural_implications.before: Effort spent reaching a working implementation; the first design was expensive and therefore treated as an endpoint.
architectural_implications.consequence: Harnesses should optimize for fast critique-revise loops over agent output (diff review, opinion injection, constraint checking) rather than for one-shot generation quality.
architectural_implications.observation: Value shifts from producing the first working design to critiquing and iterating past the generic one.

article_ideas.angle: Treat the reuse search as a pipeline stage with a cost model and a blocking gate, and show how the cheapest local action produces the most expensive global outcome.
article_ideas.audience: Platform and developer-tooling engineers, engineering managers, agent-harness builders
article_ideas.based_on: Building became cheaper than searching, leading to an explosion of redundant AI software.
article_ideas.thesis: The build-first reflex is not a discipline failure but a rational local response to an asymmetric cost change: generation collapsed in cost while evaluation and reuse discovery did not, so the pipeline's bottleneck silently migrated to the stage nobody instrumented. The fix is a first-class, enforced selection stage ahead of generation, not a reminder to search more.
article_ideas.title: Generation got cheap, selection did not: why agentic pipelines over-produce and under-choose

article_ideas.angle: Use the convergence exhibit (identical implementations appearing independently) as the argument, then redirect design-review effort from authoring quality to domain classification and input design.
article_ideas.based_on: Most AI-assisted software projects converge on the exact same median architecture.
article_ideas.thesis: When the same model and agent stack produces the same competent design across independent teams, implementation detail stops carrying information about team quality and stops functioning as advantage. Architectural differentiation inside commodity domains is a category error; the durable assets are the inputs the harness cannot reproduce - proprietary context, opinionated constraints, and distribution.
article_ideas.title: Your architecture is not the moat; the harness already knows it

article_ideas.angle: Frame the novelty budget as an allocation rule with an operational test: name the novel mechanism, name what the default path gets wrong, and accept the median everywhere else on purpose.
article_ideas.based_on: You get about one unit of true novelty per project.
article_ideas.thesis: If roughly one unit of true novelty exists per project, then evening out engineering effort across the stack is a misallocation, and the correct posture is a commodity substrate plus a deliberately protected novel core. article_ideas.title: One unit of novelty: budgeting the only scarce input left

connections.relationship: The median is the observable artifact of zero-marginal-cost generation: when the same harness produces the same design, the resulting common implementation is the median.
The reflex is the behavioral consequence of generation cost dropping below search cost; it is a rational local response with an irrational aggregate outcome.
Both reserve scarce resources for non-reproducible assets: novelty budget allocates engineering attention, distribution moat identifies where non-reproducible advantage actually lives.
Opinion is the mechanism for deviating from the default path; the median has no opinion, so explicit constraints are how output leaves the median.
The identical calculators are the empirical exhibit for the claim that the tooling stack, not the author, sets the design.

evidence_quotes.text: Most AI-assisted software projects converge on the exact same median architecture.
Nobody copied anyone; independent developers converged on the exact same median calculator because the prompt/tooling stack dictated the outcome.
Team variance and unique judgement inputs are compressed by standardized LLMs.

core_insights.generalization: Any capability generated by a standardized model+harness distribution has low inter-team variance; variance only reappears where the inputs (context, data, opinions, constraints) are non-standard.
core_insights.insight: Independent developers using the same LLM + agent harness converge on functionally identical implementations for common problems (RAG, token calculators); the convergence comes from the tooling stack dictating the design, not from copying.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If output is largely a function of harness + prompt rather than team, then architectural choices inside commodity domains carry no information about team quality and cannot function as differentiation — effort spent tuning prompt chains/agent architecture on solved problems is spend toward the median.

evidence_quotes.text: Novelty is scarce and expensive; the median is free and abundant.
You get about one unit of true novelty per project.
Google Search in 1998 combining a basic crawler/index with PageRank novelty.

core_insights.generalization: Decompose a system into a commodity substrate plus a minimal novel core; measure success on the core, and stop measuring/optimizing the substrate.
core_insights.insight: Novelty is a scarce, budgeted resource — roughly one unit of true novelty per project — while everything else should be sourced or accepted as median. The 1998 Google example frames it as one novel idea (PageRank) sitting on a fully commodity base (crawler + index).
core_insights.why_it_matters: Gives an allocation rule for scarce engineering attention: spend the novelty budget on the single differentiating mechanism and deliberately accept commodity implementations everywhere else, instead of distributing effort evenly across the stack.

evidence_quotes.text: Building became cheaper than searching, leading to an explosion of redundant AI software.
Because coding agents make building feel effortless, developers immediately start coding rather than evaluating existing open-source ecosystems.
The agent built a textbook median RAG system instantly, but completely ignored mature open-source options.

core_insights.generalization: When generation cost drops faster than evaluation cost, systems over-generate and under-select; the bottleneck migrates to retrieval/evaluation and must be instrumented as a first-class stage.
core_insights.insight: The economics of building inverted: agentic code generation made building cheaper than searching, so the default developer behavior became prompt-to-build, producing a large volume of redundant software that ignores mature open-source alternatives.
core_insights.why_it_matters: The search/evaluation step didn't get cheaper at the same rate as generation, so it is now systematically skipped — meaning the cheapest action locally produces the most expensive outcome globally (maintained, undifferentiated code). Explicit gates are needed to reinsert search into pipelines.

evidence_quotes.text: Who has already done this? What do I have that they do not? Where will this live?
Demos are expensive ways to learn you have no distribution.

core_insights.generalization: Any autonomous build step should be preceded by an explicit reuse check, a differential-advantage check, and a delivery-surface check; absent all three, generation should be blocked, not merely discouraged.
core_insights.insight: A three-question gate before invoking a coding agent: who has already done this, what do I have that they do not, and where will this live. The third question (placement/distribution) is a gate, not a detail — demos without distribution are framed as an expensive way to learn you have no users.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Converts a strategy claim into a cheap pre-flight check that can be embedded in a workflow before any agent run, catching the highest-cost error (building something with no distribution path) at the lowest-cost moment.

evidence_quotes.text: Prompt to production is the median path; decide what's wrong with it and build past it.
When AI says done, the last design is free; your job is the next one.
Be highly opinionated (the median has no opinion).

core_insights.generalization: As harnesses absorb the construction stage, the engineer's artifact shifts from code to opinion artifacts — constraints, specifications, and post-generation corrections that the generic pipeline cannot produce.
core_insights.insight: 'Prompt to production' — the standard agent workflow that takes a spec to working software — is itself the median path; differentiation requires deliberately identifying what is wrong with that default output and building past it, plus injecting an opinion where the median has none.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Locates the human/architecture contribution at the deviation layer, not the construction layer: the agent produces design N, and the value-add is design N+1 plus the explicit constraints that make the output non-generic.

evidence_quotes.text: When everyone has access to the same AI models and agents, the software itself ceases to be a competitive advantage.
Accept that standard software development is commoditized and priced near zero.
Leverage distribution and avoid building endless demos without distribution.

core_insights.insight: When every team has the same models and agents, the generated software stops being a competitive advantage; the moat relocates to distribution and unique human judgement rather than the AI wrapper or its implementation details.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Shifts where to invest for durability: acquisition surface, proprietary data/domain insight, and judgement inputs, rather than model choice, prompt design, or agent topology — which are available to every competitor at equal cost.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Hariprasad Sudharshan
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: The commoditization of AI software development and the difference between novelty and the median.
  • Purpose: To help product leaders and engineers understand how AI changes software development economics, why building everything from scratch is a trap, and where true differentiation lies. Hariprasad Sudharshan reflects on two years of building AI applications like RAG systems and token calculators, discovering that despite spending countless hours on custom architectures, prompt chains, and agent design, anyone else using modern AI coding agents arrives at essentially the same median solution. He argues that novelty is scarce and expensive, whereas the median AI software and capabilities are now free and commoditized. He offers practical frameworks for product teams to navigate the AI age, emphasizing that teams should be highly opinionated, leverage existing open-source and agent capabilities rather than reinventing deterministic infrastructure, and focus their scarce novelty budget on truly differentiated ideas.

Topic Map

The Median Software Phenomenon

  • Explanation: Explaining how AI coding agents and LLMs lead independent developers and teams to independently converge on identical solutions for common problems like RAG and token calculators.
  • Key claims:
    • Most AI-assisted software projects converge on the exact same median architecture.
    • The median software is free, commoditized, and built 230 times a minute by coding agents.
    • Team variance and unique judgement inputs are compressed by standardized LLMs.
  • Examples:
    • 244 GitHub repositories matching LLM cost calculators with identical shapes and outputs.
  • Terminology:
    • the median
    • AI slop
    • commoditized capabilities
  • Why it matters: Understanding that standard AI tooling gives everyone identical median output prevents organizations from mistaking commoditized AI wrappers for unique competitive moats.

Novelty vs. The Median in the Age of AI

  • Explanation: Contrasting the scarce element of true novelty with the ubiquitous and accessible median capabilities generated by AI models and harnesses.
  • Key claims:
    • Novelty is scarce and expensive; the median is free and abundant.
    • You get about one unit of true novelty per project.
    • Spending time optimizing prompt chains and agent architecture on common problems yields median results.
  • Examples:
    • Google Search in 1998 combining a basic crawler/index with PageRank novelty.
  • Terminology:
    • novelty budget
    • first principles
    • moat
  • Why it matters: Teams must consciously allocate their scarce novelty budget toward truly unique product features rather than reinventing solved problems.

The Build-First Reflex and Three Questions

  • Explanation: Examining the modern reflex to immediately prompt coding agents to build everything rather than searching for existing open-source solutions, and introducing a three-question playbook.
  • Key claims:
    • Building became cheaper than searching, leading to an explosion of redundant AI software.
    • Leaders must ask three questions before prompting a coding agent: Who has already done this? What do I have that they do not? Where will this live?
    • Demos are expensive ways to learn you have no distribution.
  • Examples:
    • Building a custom RAG system over PDFs when thousands of mature open-source alternatives exist.
  • Terminology:
    • build-first reflex
    • distribution moat
    • scaffolding
  • Why it matters: Saves engineering teams wasted effort building redundant software and forces focus on distribution and unique value.

Key Points

Novelty is scarce, the median is free

  • Explanation: AI models and coding agents have commoditized standard software development, making the median output universally accessible and free.
  • Evidence: Over 1.1 million public repos importing LLM SDKs and 4.3 million AI-related repositories showing convergent solutions.
  • Practical implication: Do not waste limited engineering bandwidth reinventing standard tools; focus entirely on what makes your product uniquely novel.

The danger of the build-first reflex

  • Explanation: Because coding agents make building feel effortless, developers immediately start coding rather than evaluating existing open-source ecosystems.
  • Evidence: Building a custom RAG or calculator in two hours only to find hundreds of identical implementations.
  • Practical implication: Adopt rigorous search and evaluation habits before letting AI agents generate redundant codebases.

Distribution is the moat, not the AI wrapper

  • Explanation: When everyone has access to the same AI models and agents, the software itself ceases to be a competitive advantage.
  • Evidence: GitHub stats showing hundreds of identical LLM cost calculators created by independent developers.
  • Practical implication: Focus on distribution, user acquisition moats, and unique human judgment rather than software implementation details.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Three Questions Before Prompting a Coding Agent

  • How it works: A strategic checklist for engineering leaders and product teams before delegating development to AI agents.
  • Components:
    • Who has already done this?
    • What do I have that they do not?
    • Where will this live?
  • When to use: Before starting any new AI-assisted software development project or feature build.

Four Ways Past the Median

  • How it works: Four guiding principles to achieve true product differentiation in an era of commoditized AI software.
  • Components:
    • Be highly opinionated (the median has no opinion).
    • Prompt to production is the median path; decide what's wrong with it and build past it.
    • When AI says done, the last design is free; your job is the next one.
    • Leverage distribution and avoid building endless demos without distribution.
  • When to use: When planning product roadmaps and evaluating whether a feature is genuinely novel.

Examples & Case Studies

Spent two years building and refining a token calculator app across multiple AI platforms, sacrificing social time and sleep.

  • Illustrates: The build-first reflex and the pursuit of the median.
  • Lesson: Nobody copied anyone; independent developers converged on the exact same median calculator because the prompt/tooling stack dictated the outcome.

Asked an AI agent to build a RAG system over PDFs without checking open-source alternatives.

  • Illustrates: The ease of generating standard software via AI coding agents.
  • Lesson: The agent built a textbook median RAG system instantly, but completely ignored mature open-source options.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Ask the three strategic questions before instructing a coding agent to build.
    • Audit your product roadmap for true novelty versus commoditized features.
    • Stop treating AI-generated median software as a unique differentiator.
  • Strategic:
    • Allocate your novelty budget to architecture, unique domain insights, or distribution moats.
    • Accept that standard software development is commoditized and priced near zero.
    • Focus on distribution and human judgment as primary competitive advantages.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • What is the single unit of true novelty in our current product?
    • Are we building a commodity wrapper that any competitor can generate with a prompt?
    • Do we have a distribution moat or are we just building expensive demos?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • 80% of new GitHub developers use Copilot in their first week. (statistic)
  • Over 1.1 million public repos import LLM SDKs. (statistic)
  • The modern world's GDP is driven by deterministic software. (economic argument)

Notable Quotes

"The modern world runs on it. Every dollar of GDP stops without it." "Novelty is scarce. The median is free." "You get about one unit of true novelty per project." "You build intuition by building."

Compressed Summary

  • AI coding agents commoditize standard software development into a universal median.
  • Novelty is scarce and expensive; teams get roughly one unit of true novelty per project.
  • The build-first reflex leads teams to generate redundant software without checking existing solutions.
  • Distribution and human judgment remain the true competitive moats in the age of AI.
  • Keywords: median, novelty, commoditization, agents, software
  • Core insight: In the age of AI, standard software development is commoditized into a free median, forcing teams to reserve their scarce novelty budget for true differentiation.

  - Be highly opinionated (the median has no opinion).
  - Prompt to production is the median path; decide what's wrong with it and build past it.
  - When AI says done, the last design is free; your job is the next one.
  - Leverage distribution and avoid building endless demos without distribution.
- **When to use**: When planning product roadmaps and evaluating whether a feature is genuinely novel.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Spent two years building and refining a token calculator app across multiple AI platforms, sacrificing social time and sleep.
- **Illustrates**: The build-first reflex and the pursuit of the median.
- **Lesson**: Nobody copied anyone; independent developers converged on the exact same median calculator because the prompt/tooling stack dictated the outcome.
### Asked an AI agent to build a RAG system over PDFs without checking open-source alternatives.
- **Illustrates**: The ease of generating standard software via AI coding agents.
- **Lesson**: The agent built a textbook median RAG system instantly, but completely ignored mature open-source options.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Ask the three strategic questions before instructing a coding agent to build.
  - Audit your product roadmap for true novelty versus commoditized features.
  - Stop treating AI-generated median software as a unique differentiator.
- **Strategic**:
  - Allocate your novelty budget to architecture, unique domain insights, or distribution moats.
  - Accept that standard software development is commoditized and priced near zero.
  - Focus on distribution and human judgment as primary competitive advantages.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - What is the single unit of true novelty in our current product?
  - Are we building a commodity wrapper that any competitor can generate with a prompt?
  - Do we have a distribution moat or are we just building expensive demos?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- 80% of new GitHub developers use Copilot in their first week. (statistic)
- Over 1.1 million public repos import LLM SDKs. (statistic)
- The modern world's GDP is driven by deterministic software. (economic argument)
## Notable Quotes
> "The modern world runs on it. Every dollar of GDP stops without it."
> "Novelty is scarce. The median is free."
> "You get about one unit of true novelty per project."
> "You build intuition by building."
## Compressed Summary
- AI coding agents commoditize standard software development into a universal median.
- Novelty is scarce and expensive; teams get roughly one unit of true novelty per project.
- The build-first reflex leads teams to generate redundant software without checking existing solutions.
- Distribution and human judgment remain the true competitive moats in the age of AI.
- **Keywords**: median, novelty, commoditization, agents, software
- **Core insight**: In the age of AI, standard software development is commoditized into a free median, forcing teams to reserve their scarce novelty budget for true differentiation.
